needs_redesign.capability: Driver-contributed dashboard cards (runtime plugin registry + declarative CardElement rendering)
needs_redesign.why: Android discovers plugins at runtime through a ConcurrentHashMap-backed `PluginRegistry` and renders their cards from a declarative `DashboardCardDescriptor`/`CardElement` tree precisely BECAUSE the plugin code is dynamically loaded and must not touch host UI. On iOS, drivers are compile-time-linked Swift modules (App Store Guideline 2.5.2 forbids dynamic code loading), so runtime discovery, the undefined iteration order it caused, and the sandboxing rationale for a data-only UI contract all change. The user-visible outcome (cards below the core cards, ordered by ascending priority, tappable when hasDetail) must be preserved exactly.
options: Keep the declarative descriptor contract: each linked driver module conforms to a `DashboardCardProviding` protocol vending `AsyncSequence<[DashboardCardDescriptor]>`, and one host renderer maps CardElement cases to SwiftUI views. Registry becomes a static array assembled at app launch.
Let each driver module vend a SwiftUI `View` directly, dropping CardElement entirely — simpler and more expressive, but couples driver modules to SwiftUI and to the host's design system.
Hybrid: descriptors for the shipped drivers, with an escape hatch for a module to supply a custom View.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Keep the declarative descriptor contract (option 1). It costs almost nothing to port (CardElement is a 9-case sum type with trivial preconditions), it keeps driver modules free of any UI framework so the SAME module can feed the watchOS app and future surfaces, and it preserves the priority/id/title/hasDetail contract the backend and the E2E identifiers (`plugin_card_<id>`) already encode. Keep the explicit sort of active module IDs even though a static array is deterministic — it costs nothing and keeps phone/Watch badge order identical.

needs_redesign.capability: Dashboard data flows, settings reconciliation, and manual refresh under the iOS app lifecycle
needs_redesign.why: The dashboard's freshness assumptions rest on Android's foreground-service poll loop (15 s fast poll for IoB/basal/CGM, which is also a BLE keep-alive because the pump drops idle links at ~30 s). iOS has no foreground service. Once the app is backgrounded it is suspended within seconds; the only background execution available is (a) Core Bluetooth wake-ups via `UIBackgroundModes: bluetooth-central` + `CBCentralManagerOptionRestoreIdentifierKey`, which fire on connect/disconnect and on characteristic notifications for peripherals you have an outstanding connect request for — never on a timer — and (b) `BGAppRefreshTask`, which is opportunistic, budgeted by usage, and typically minutes-to-hours apart. So the 15 s cadence and the ~30 s keep-alive cannot both be guaranteed, and the dashboard must therefore treat 'the app was suspended' as a first-class state rather than assuming continuous polling.
options: Foreground-only polling parity: run the 15 s stagger loop only while the app is active; on every `scenePhase == .active` transition immediately re-run the full refresh sequence, and render whatever freshness tier the data actually earns (often TOO_STALE after a long background). Background continuity is left to CB state restoration + notify-characteristic pushes from the pump and to backend push where a backend exists.

Pursue continuous background BLE: keep a subscription to a notifying pump characteristic so the pump pushes data and iOS wakes the app per notification, with CB state restoration to survive termination. Preserves near-continuous freshness for pumps that notify, but is entirely dependent on each driver's protocol supporting notifications and cannot be validated in the Simulator at all.

Backend-driven continuity: when a backend is configured, have it push new readings via APNs (with `content-available` background pushes or, for the alert path, alert pushes) so the phone re-hydrates without BLE. Does nothing for BLE-only users.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Do all three, layered, with option 1 as the load-bearing contract. Foreground behaviour is the parity surface and must be exact (same order, same 500 ms stagger, same concurrent-refresh drop via a compare-and-swap flag, same 'CGM result also goes through the polling orchestrator so a manual refresh reaches the alert floor'). Add an explicit scenePhase-active refresh so returning to the app never shows a value the app could have refreshed but didn't. Then let each driver module opt into notify-characteristic background delivery, and let backend-configured users additionally receive push. Critically: do NOT let the display layer paper over the gap — if the data is 40 minutes old because iOS suspended the app, the hero must be grey with 'Too old', which is exactly what the ported freshness policy already does.

needs_redesign.capability: Reactive settings transport across the app, its widget/complication extensions, and the Watch app
needs_redesign.why: Android uses a SharedPreferences `OnSharedPreferenceChangeListener` callbackFlow as the reactive transport for glucose unit, theme, thresholds, retention, debug toggles and category labels — one process, instant propagation. On iOS the same values are needed by at least three processes on two devices: the app, its WidgetKit extension(s) (Lock Screen / Home Screen / Smart Stack / watch complications), and the watchOS app. `UserDefaults(suiteName:)` in an App Group shares storage between the app and its extensions on the SAME device, but `UserDefaults.didChangeNotification` does not reliably fire cross-process, and App Groups do not span the phone↔Watch boundary at all.
options: App Group UserDefaults for app↔extensions, with the app calling `WidgetCenter.shared.reloadTimelines(ofKind:)` on every settings write; WatchConnectivity `updateApplicationContext` (latest-value-wins, queued while the counterpart is unreachable) for app→Watch, with the Watch mirroring into its own App Group defaults and reloading its complications.
Put settings in the shared GRDB database inside the App Group and observe it with `ValueObservation` from every on-device process, still using WatchConnectivity for the phone→Watch hop.
Treat settings as backend state and have each surface fetch independently — breaks the BLE-only mode entirely.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1. `updateApplicationContext` is the right WatchConnectivity primitive for settings (it coalesces, survives the counterpart being unreachable, and delivers on next wake), and explicit `WidgetCenter` reloads are the only supported way to make an extension notice a defaults change. The PRD requirement is behavioural, not mechanical: a unit or theme change made anywhere must reach every surface without an app restart, and no surface may ever display a value in a different unit from the phone.

needs_redesign.capability: Freshness ticking on watchOS complications, Smart Stack, and Lock Screen widgets
needs_redesign.why: The single most safety-load-bearing behaviour in this subsystem is that the FRESH→STALE→TOO_STALE degrade happens on a wall-clock ticker WITHOUT new data arriving, so a dead sensor cannot leave a confident green number on screen. In-app that is a `TimelineView` and ports cleanly. On every widget/complication surface it cannot be: WidgetKit is a pull model with a hard reload budget (roughly 40–70 timeline reloads per day for a placed iOS widget; watchOS complications for the active face get more but are still budgeted), and a widget process cannot run a timer.
options: Encode the degrade in the timeline itself: every `getTimeline` returns entries at now, at `timestamp + staleAfterMs`, and at `timestamp + tooStaleAfterMs`, each pre-rendered in the correct tier (coloured → amber-with-badge → grey-with-'Too old'). WidgetKit renders entries at their scheduled dates without waking the extension, so the degrade is exact and costs zero budget.
Rely on frequent `reloadTimelines` calls from the app whenever new data arrives — burns budget, and does nothing when the app is suspended, which is precisely when the degrade matters.
Show no freshness state on complications, only the value — unacceptable: it recreates the exact failure the policy exists to prevent.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1, and make it a hard PRD requirement. It is a perfect structural fit: WidgetKit's timeline model was designed for exactly this. Every complication and widget timeline must contain the two boundary entries derived from the same shared `FreshnessPolicy` the phone uses, so a complication whose data stops arriving turns grey at the 15-minute mark on its own. Also add `.privacySensitive()` where appropriate and handle `redactionReasons` for watchOS Always-On (SwiftUI throttles AOD updates to roughly once per minute and dims the UI — the age caption must remain legible and honest under redaction).

needs_redesign.why: Android sets `Activity.requestedOrientation = SCREEN_ORIENTATION_SENSOR_LANDSCAPE` on enter and restores it on dispose. iOS has no per-screen orientation property on a SwiftUI view; orientation is negotiated between the Info.plist `UISupportedInterfaceOrientations`, the root view controller's `supportedInterfaceOrientations`, and (iOS 16+) `UIWindowScene.requestGeometryUpdate(.iOS(interfaceOrientations:))` paired with `setNeedsUpdateOfSupportedInterfaceOrientations()`. There is also no 'sensor landscape' concept, and the interaction with the user's Portrait Orientation Lock is a HIG sensitivity Android does not have.
options: Reproduce the lock: a `UIViewControllerRepresentable` (or an AppDelegate-held orientation mask) that widens the supported mask to `.landscape` on appear, calls `requestGeometryUpdate(.iOS(interfaceOrientations: .landscape))`, and narrows it back on disappear. Requires `UISupportedInterfaceOrientations` to include both landscape values.

Make the detail chart orientation-agnostic: a full-screen chart that lays out well in portrait and simply rotates with the device, relying on the existing pinch/pan to get the same effective resolution.
Auto-rotate on entry but do not force: widen the mask so landscape becomes available on the detail screen only, and let the user turn the phone.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1 for parity — the wide chart genuinely needs the landscape aspect ratio and the Android UX made that call deliberately. Implement it via `requestGeometryUpdate`, which does override the device rotation lock when the app's declared orientations permit it, and always restore the previous mask on dismissal (an unrestored mask is a classic iOS bug). Keep the graceful-degradation posture Android has: if the window scene is unavailable, log and skip rather than crashing. Note that this constrains the app to iPhone; on iPad the orientation request is not honoured the same way.

needs_redesign.capability: Numeric locale and rounding consistency across the dashboard
needs_redesign.why: Two separate defects compound on iOS. (1) Android forces Locale.US inside GlucoseFormat but uses the DEVICE locale for IoB, basal, battery, reservoir, TIR percentages, CV%, GMI and their accessibility strings — so a comma-decimal device today mixes '6.7 mmol/L' with '1,23u'. (2) More seriously, Java's Formatter documents `%f` as HALF_UP on the decimal expansion, while C/Foundation `String(format:)` rounds the exact binary value half-to-EVEN. That is not theoretical: a TIR bucket of exactly 12.5% renders '13%' on Android and '12%' in a naive Swift port, and a mean glucose of exactly 100.5 renders '101' vs '100'. Any per-value cross-surface comparison would silently drift.
options: Dot-decimal everywhere on the dashboard (extend the GlucoseFormat rule to every displayed number), with explicit half-up rounding for every formatted value. Fixes the Android mixed-separator inconsistency and guarantees cross-surface string equality.
Locale-aware everywhere except glucose. Preserves the Android inconsistency verbatim, including the mixed-separator screen.
Locale-aware everywhere including glucose. Forbidden — it breaks the pinned cross-surface mmol fixture, the phone/Watch equality contract, and the release log scrubber.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1. Use `Locale(identifier: "en_US_POSIX")` and explicit half-up rounding (`Decimal` with `.plain`, or `NumberFormatter` with `roundingMode = .halfUp` — note NumberFormatter defaults to `.halfEven`) for every number the dashboard renders, and pin the exact-tie cases (12.5%, 100.5 mean, 0.125 U) in tests against the Android strings. This is a deliberate, documented improvement over Android rather than a defect port, and it is the only option that keeps the phone, the Watch, the widgets and the backend emitting identical strings.

needs_redesign.capability: Cleartext / local-network access to a self-hosted backend (the surface behind the insecure-HTTP banner)
needs_redesign.why: The banner itself ports trivially, but the capability it warns about does not. iOS App Transport Security blocks cleartext HTTP by default and requires an explicit Info.plist posture; separately, iOS 14+ Local Network Privacy requires `NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription` and shows a user permission prompt before ANY connection to a local-network host, including a self-hosted backend on 192.168.x.x or a `.local` name. Android needed neither. A denied local-network permission is a silent, unrecoverable-in-app failure mode (the user must re-enable it in Settings) that the status row and banner have no state for today. Crucially, the iOS Simulator does not enforce Local Network Privacy — it uses the Mac's networking — so this path CANNOT be validated in the Simulator and will only fail on device.
options: `NSAllowsLocalNetworking = true` plus `NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription`, restricting self-hosted servers to `.local`/unqualified hostnames and link-local addresses; anything else must be HTTPS.

`NSAllowsArbitraryLoads = true` plus `NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription`, permitting any user-entered host over cleartext. Broadest compatibility with existing self-hosted setups, but requires a written justification at App Review and weakens the app's default posture.
HTTPS-only for the backend, dropping the insecure-LAN-HTTP escape hatch entirely and requiring users to terminate TLS (self-signed certs with a trust prompt, or a reverse proxy).
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1 as the shipped default, with the existing 'I understand the risk' acknowledgement gate extended to also explain the iOS local-network permission, plus a new honest status: the reachability indicator must distinguish 'local network permission denied' from 'backend unreachable', with a tap target that deep-links to `UIApplication.openSettingsURLString`. Do not reach for `NSAllowsArbitraryLoads` unless field testing proves option 1 excludes real self-hosted setups — it invites an App Review conversation for a capability most users will not need. Whichever is chosen, add `NSBonjourServices` if any discovery is done, and make the Simulator's non-enforcement an explicit note in the dev-loop docs so the developer tests this path on hardware before every TestFlight upload.

impossible.capability: A persistent, non-dismissible OS-level status surface mirroring the Android foreground-service notification ('Connected to pump' / 'Server alerts paused' / 'Floor watching' / 'Floor NOT watching')
impossible.why: iOS has no ongoing or non-dismissible notification. `UNNotificationRequest` produces a user-dismissible banner; there is no `setOngoing(true)` equivalent and no persistent notification tied to app execution, because there is no foreground service to tie it to. Live Activities are the nearest construct and they are explicitly time-bounded and user-dismissible: an activity runs at most 8 hours active plus roughly 4 more hours on the Lock Screen before the system ends it, the user can swipe it away at any time, and starting one normally requires the app to be in the foreground (push-to-start exists from iOS 17.2 but still cannot guarantee persistence). Widgets and Smart Stack complications are budgeted pull surfaces the user must choose to place. Nothing on iOS can guarantee 'this status is always visible while the app is monitoring'.
impossible.closest_alternative: A three-part honest substitute: (1) an ActivityKit Live Activity started when a pump session begins, showing pump-link state and the alert-floor claim on the Lock Screen and Dynamic Island, refreshed via ActivityKit updates and pre-scheduled `staleDate` so it self-degrades to 'not watching' rather than going quietly wrong; (2) a Home Screen / Lock Screen widget and a watchOS complication carrying the same claim with WidgetKit timeline entries scheduled at the freshness boundaries, so the claim decays on time with zero refresh budget; (3) a one-shot, user-dismissible local notification when the floor stops watching, so the transition is announced even if no persistent surface is placed. The honesty contract must invert relative to Android: because no surface is guaranteed present, the ABSENCE of a 'watching' surface must never be read by the user as 'watching' — the in-app status row must be the authoritative claim and the onboarding copy must say so.

impossible.capability: Guaranteed fixed-cadence background refresh (Android's 15-second pump poll and the ~30-second BLE keep-alive) keeping the dashboard, complications and alert floor continuously current while the app is not in the foreground
impossible.why: iOS provides no periodic background execution to a suspended app. `BGAppRefreshTask` is opportunistic and budgeted by the system against user launch patterns — `earliestBeginDate` is a floor, not a schedule, and intervals of minutes to hours are normal; `BGProcessingTask` requires charging and device idle. Core Bluetooth's `bluetooth-central` background mode wakes the app on peripheral connection/disconnection and on value updates for characteristics you are subscribed to — it does not provide a timer, and background scanning is restricted to explicit service UUIDs with duplicate filtering forced on. There is no supported way to run a 15-second loop, and any attempt (audio session abuse, location background mode without a real location feature) is an App Review rejection under Guideline 2.5.4 and drains the battery.
impossible.closest_alternative: Compose three mechanisms and design the display to be honest about the gaps. (a) Where a driver's protocol supports it, subscribe to a notifying characteristic so the PUMP drives the cadence and iOS wakes the app per notification; combine with `CBCentralManagerOptionRestoreIdentifierKey` state preservation and restoration so the app is relaunched into the background after termination and can re-establish. (b) Register a `BGAppRefreshTask` for opportunistic settings reconciliation and sync-queue drain, never for anything the user's safety depends on. (c) For backend-configured users, have the server push new readings via APNs. Then let the ported freshness policy do its job: whatever is missed shows as STALE and then TOO_STALE on schedule, the alert floor refuses to claim it is watching, and complications degrade via pre-scheduled timeline entries. The right framing for the PRD is that iOS trades guaranteed cadence for guaranteed honesty — the app must never present a gap as continuity.

impossible.capability: Shipping a custom watch face (the Android `watchface/` module and the phone→watch face push/install flow)
impossible.why: watchOS does not support third-party watch faces. There is no API to define a face, and no mechanism for an app to install one; the Android app's WatchFaceInstaller/WatchFaceReceiveService APK-push flow has no counterpart and would in any case be dynamic code loading, which App Store Guideline 2.5.2 forbids.
impossible.closest_alternative: Two things, both real and both worth shipping. (1) WidgetKit complications for watchOS (`WidgetFamily.accessoryCircular` / `.accessoryCorner` / `.accessoryRectangular` / `.accessoryInline`) that the user adds to an Apple-provided face — this delivers the actual capability the custom face existed to provide (glucose, trend, IoB, age, and the graph as a rectangular complication rendered with the same shared `Canvas` code) and additionally reaches the Smart Stack and the iPhone Lock Screen with the same widget code. (2) Watch Face Sharing (watchOS 7+): bundle a curated `.watchface` file in the app that pre-configures an Apple face with the app's complications already placed, and offer an 'Add to Watch' button — the user taps once and gets a ready-made face. That is as close to 'we ship you a face' as the platform allows, and it is a genuinely good experience.

ios_requirements: The app must present a single scrolling Home dashboard whose card order is fixed and identical to Android: connection/sync status row, glucose hero, recent-meal glance (only when a recent meal exists), glucose trend chart, Time in Range, CGM Stats, Insulin Summary, Recent Boluses, then driver-contributed cards in ascending priority order, then a single footer line ('Pair your pump in Settings to start' when disconnected; 'Loading pump data...' when connected with no CGM value; nothing otherwise).
Every dashboard card must render even with no data, each showing its own empty-state message; no card may be hidden for lack of data.

The user must be able to pull down on Home to force an immediate refresh. A refresh must read pump values over BLE sequentially in the order IoB, basal rate, battery, reservoir, CGM with a 500 ms gap between reads, must route the CGM result through the same path the background poller uses so a manual refresh can feed the alert floor immediately, and must concurrently reconcile glucose range, glucose unit, meal-intelligence, analytics config, pump profile, safety limits and alert thresholds when a backend is configured. A refresh requested while one is in flight must be dropped, not queued.
Every time the app returns to the foreground, it must immediately re-run the pump read sequence, because iOS suspends the app in the background and the last value may be arbitrarily old.
Any reconciliation or refresh failure must be logged and must leave the previous cached values intact; no failure may blank or reset a displayed value.

The status row must show a pump-link indicator in every mode with six distinct states (connected, connecting/authenticating, reconnecting, scanning, pairing failed, disconnected), using the Android colour semantics (blue = connected, amber = transitional, red = failed or absent) and the same accompanying text, including showing NO text for the connected and disconnected resting states. The crossed-out state must be presented as a resting state, not an error.

The sync and backend-reachability indicators must be hidden entirely when no backend is configured, and in their healthy states must remain visually distinguishable from each other (a transfer/up-down glyph for sync, a cloud-with-check for reachability), so a user can tell 'my data is uploaded' from 'my server answers right now'.

Backend reachability must be derived only from traffic the app already makes: any HTTP response, including 4xx and 5xx, proves reachability; only two consecutive transport-level failures flip to unreachable. No health-check endpoint may be added. Device-offline must take precedence over backend-unreachable.
Device connectivity must not require validated internet access, so a LAN-only network reaching a self-hosted server counts as online.

When a self-hosted server is on the local network, the app must request local-network permission with a clear purpose string, and must surface a distinct, actionable status when that permission is denied — never conflating it with 'backend unreachable'.

When the app is configured to reach a server over plain HTTP, a persistent warning banner must appear above all content including onboarding, derived from the same policy that governs whether the request layer permits the connection, and enabling that mode must require an explicit risk acknowledgement.

Each active, compiled-in driver module that ships a brand mark must display it untinted after the status icons, in a horizontally scrollable strip that can never push the status icons off a narrow screen; a module without a mark stays active and shows nothing. At most one pump brand mark can ever appear.

The glucose hero must show the current value at hero scale with its trend glyph in the same colour, the unit label, a relative-age caption coloured by freshness, and the secondary metrics IoB, basal rate (with a Sleep / Exercise / Automated suffix), battery percentage and reservoir units when present. With no reading it must show '--' and the unit label only, with no age caption, badge or secondary metrics.

When the glucose reading is too stale, the hero value and trend glyph must lose their severity colour and render de-emphasised grey, gain a 'Too old' badge, and the card's spoken description must announce that the reading is stale and its age BEFORE reading out any other metric.

Glucose severity colour must be a function of the stored mg/dL value alone with no unit input, so the display-unit choice can never change the severity a user sees. The colour must encode severity, not direction: low and high share one colour, urgent-low and urgent-high share another. Boundary behaviour must match Android exactly (55 urgent-low, 56 low, 70 low, 71 in-range, 179 in-range, 180 high, 249 high, 250 urgent-high).

All storage, transport, threshold comparison, alerting, chart geometry, Time-in-Range bucketing, CV% and GMI must operate on canonical mg/dL integers. Only an enumerable set of rendered strings may convert: hero value and unit label, chart Y-axis labels, chart tooltip, TIR bucket-boundary and target labels, CGM-stats mean and standard deviation, and the bolus table's BG column.

mg/dL to mmol/L conversion must use exactly one constant, 18.0156, shared with the backend and the Apple Watch app, converting once from the most precise mg/dL source and rounding last to one decimal. No second constant may exist anywhere in the codebase.

The iPhone app and the Apple Watch app must produce byte-identical glucose strings for the same stored mg/dL value, pinned by a shared cross-surface fixture (54→3.0, 70→3.9, 99→5.5, 100→5.6, 120→6.7, 180→10.0, 250→13.9, 400→22.2, 20→1.1, 500→27.8).

Glucose spreads (standard deviations and differences) must convert through a distinct, offset-free path and always render with one decimal in either unit; the value converter must never be used for a spread.

Every number the dashboard displays must use a dot decimal separator and half-up rounding regardless of device locale, so no screen mixes separators and no percentage, mean or unit value differs by a digit from the equivalent Android string.

Changing the glucose unit anywhere — in Settings or via a backend reconcile — must re-render every glucose surface on the phone and propagate to the Watch app and every complication and widget without an app restart. The unit must be reconciled from the backend on every dashboard load, never gated behind another setting's staleness clock.

Data freshness must be classified into fresh / stale / too-stale using half-open boundaries (exactly at a threshold crosses into the worse tier) with per-source policies: CGM stale at 6 minutes and too-stale at 15; pump metrics (IoB, basal, battery, reservoir) stale at 15 minutes and too-stale at 60. Negative ages classify as fresh for display purposes only.

Freshness must re-evaluate on a wall-clock timer independent of new data arriving, at one quarter of the source's stale threshold clamped to 2–30 seconds, so a staleness badge appears and the age caption grows while the app sits open and no new reading arrives.

A staleness badge must render nothing at all when fresh, 'Stale' in amber when stale, and 'Too old' in grey when too-stale — such that a fully fresh screen contains zero staleness-badge elements as an assertable test invariant.

On every Apple Watch complication, Smart Stack entry and Lock Screen or Home Screen widget, the fresh→stale→too-stale degrade must be pre-scheduled as timeline entries at the exact policy boundaries computed from the reading's own timestamp, so the surface degrades on time even when the extension is never woken with new data.

The alert-floor gate must require strictly-fresh data measured against the CGM's own sensor timestamp — never a poll, receive or wall-clock time — must tolerate up to 60 seconds of future skew, and must be the single shared definition used by display, alerting and any 'this device is watching you' claim. Stale and too-stale must both suppress the alarm and flip the claim to an honest 'not watching'.

Any 'this device is watching' claim must decay on its own schedule with no new data, must emit a pessimistic value first when its inputs are still unknown, and must be designed to under-claim rather than over-claim. Because iOS provides no guaranteed-persistent status surface, the absence of a widget, complication or Live Activity must never be presentable to the user as evidence that monitoring is active.

The trend chart must render on a fixed 40–300 mg/dL Y axis with dashed grid lines and labels only at the low, high and urgent-high thresholds converted to the user's unit, over a translucent target-range band. Readings outside the axis must be pinned to the edge while keeping their true severity colour. Glucose must be drawn as unconnected dots, on top of every overlay.

The chart must draw, back to front: target band, threshold grid lines, Y-axis labels, X-axis time labels, sleep/exercise mode bands, the stepped basal area occupying the bottom quarter of the plot, the IoB area and line on an independent right-hand scale, staggered diamond bolus markers with unit and type labels, then glucose dots.

Chart time-axis label format and tick count must follow the visible span using the Android rules, and the chart must abort drawing safely on a zero-span or zero-size plot area rather than dividing by zero.
The chart legend must list only the series actually present in the loaded data.

From Home the user must be able to expand the chart into a detail view supporting pinch-zoom down to a 15-minute minimum span and no wider than the selected period, drag-pan bounded by the period start and 'now', double-tap to reset the viewport, and tap-to-inspect a reading via a tooltip showing the value with its unit label and the local time — accepting a tap only within 3% of the visible span (clamped to 1–5 minutes) of a reading, and dismissing the tooltip on any other gesture.
The chart detail view must present in landscape and must restore the previous orientation posture on exit.

Period selection must be shared between the Home chart card and the chart detail view, and between the Recent Boluses card and the Bolus History screen, so a change made in one is reflected in the other.

The dashboard must maintain five independent period selections (chart, Time in Range, CGM stats, insulin summary, bolus list) with the Android defaults, and must preserve the distinction that Time in Range and CGM stats use rolling now-minus-N-hours windows while insulin summary and bolus lists use day-boundary-aligned windows anchored on a configurable day-boundary hour.

Period choices must be filtered by the user's local retention setting, and a selection outside the available set must fall back to the first available period; the CGM Stats card must additionally push the corrected selection back into shared state.

Time in Range must be computed by a database aggregate over readings between 20 and 500 mg/dL using the Android bucket comparisons, and rendered as a five-segment stacked bar in which the last non-zero segment absorbs all rounding, with a legend labelling bucket boundaries in the user's unit, a target caption in the user's unit, and a quality assessment label.

CGM statistics must report mean, sample standard deviation using the n−1 denominator, CV%, GMI, CGM-active percentage against an expectation of 12 readings per hour, and the valid reading count, with the Android quality bands. GMI and CV% must be derived from the raw mg/dL mean and must never be unit-converted.

Insulin summary must report total daily dose, the basal/bolus split as a stacked bar and legend, food and correction portions per day, and a per-category breakdown in a fixed display order. Basal must be computed as a segment integral with each segment capped at two hours and the final segment extended to now, against a denominator measured from now and floored at one day, so gaps under-report rather than extrapolate.

The app must not present a bolus's requested meal and correction portions as if they summed to the delivered units; partial delivery, cancellation and automated boluses can legitimately break that identity.

Recent Boluses must show the five most recent events in descending time order with time, units, a type badge, BG at event and IoB at event, plus a derived plain-language reason, and must offer a path to a full Bolus History screen listing all events for the period.

BG at event and IoB at event must be cross-referenced to the nearest reading within plus or minus five minutes, showing '--' when no reading falls in that window. The BG column must render in the user's display unit with a unit label — a deliberate correction of the current Android behaviour, which prints a raw mg/dL integer to mmol/L users.

Glucose thresholds must be cached locally with the defaults 55/70/180/250, refreshed from the backend when older than 15 minutes, each value coerced into 20–500, and the entire update rejected — leaving the previous values intact — when the ordering invariant fails. Thresholds must remain mg/dL on the wire and in storage regardless of the display unit.

Glucose readings outside 20–500 mg/dL and boluses outside 0–25 units must be rejected at the model boundary and silently skipped when read back from local storage, never surfaced as an error row; the dashboard must fall back to the next valid reading or to the no-data state.

Local pump and CGM data must be encrypted at rest using the platform's data protection so it is unreadable before first device unlock, and credentials must be stored in the Keychain with an accessibility class that permits background use.

The tab bar must be capability-driven: Home, Alerts and Settings always present, and an AI Chat tab only when a backend is configured. Backend-only destinations must remain registered so restored navigation state and deep links resolve, redirecting to Home rather than blanking when no backend is configured, and the backend-configured decision must be evaluated live rather than captured when the navigation graph is built.
The start destination must depend only on onboarding completion and never on session validity, so an expired or absent session still reaches locally stored pump and CGM data offline.

A tappable session banner must appear for an expired session unconditionally, and for an unauthenticated state only when a backend is configured, and must never appear while authentication state is still initialising. It must not appear during onboarding.
Detail screens must hide the tab bar and provide a back affordance.

The app must support System, Dark and Light theme selection, applying it live without restart, using the Android palette exactly. Semantic colours (glucose severity, bolus type, meal confidence, and the amber safety-note treatment that must never be the error red) must be identical in both appearances, and the safety-note treatment must resolve against the effective theme so a forced Light or Dark selection is respected.
Every element that carries a Compose test tag today must carry the same string as an accessibility identifier, and 'a fresh screen contains zero staleness badges' must remain an assertable condition.

Every card must expose a single combined VoiceOver description matching the Android content-description text, with glucose values spoken in the user's unit using the spoken unit names ('milligrams per deciliter' / 'millimoles per liter').
The hero value and other fixed-size numerals must remain legible and non-truncating across Dynamic Type sizes including the accessibility sizes.

Markdown prose rendered anywhere in the app must strip image markdown and HTML image tags before rendering so no outbound image fetch can be triggered by generated content, and must only open http and https links.

Every 'now' used by freshness classification, chart windows, day-boundary alignment, the basal integral and the TDD denominator must come from an injectable clock rather than a direct system-time read, so the entire time-dependent surface can be exercised deterministically — the iOS Simulator cannot have its clock changed independently of the host Mac.

Debug builds must include a simulated pump driver, selectable in the Simulator, that can drive every connection state, replay recorded CGM / IoB / basal / bolus histories, and inject stale, out-of-range, future-dated and clock-rewound values — because Core Bluetooth does not exist in the iOS Simulator and no BLE-dependent state on this dashboard can otherwise be reached during development.

Debug builds must retain the compressed fast-staleness policy (stale at 20 seconds, too-stale at 45 seconds) behind a toggle that is hard-gated so it can never be reached in a TestFlight or Release build.

The Apple Watch app and the iPhone app must link the same formatting, freshness and threshold modules rather than reimplementing them, so a drift in either is a compile-time impossibility rather than a test that someone forgot to run.

risks.risk: Numeric rounding divergence between Java's HALF_UP formatter and C/Foundation's round-half-to-even. A Time-in-Range bucket of exactly 12.5% renders '13%' on Android and '12%' in a naive Swift port; a mean glucose of exactly 100.5 renders '101' vs '100'. These are reachable with small reading counts, and the glucose mmol fixture only passes by luck (no tie is reachable in the 20–500 range for the 18.0156 divisor).
risks.mitigation: Route every displayed number through one formatting helper that uses en_US_POSIX and explicit half-up rounding (Decimal with .plain, or NumberFormatter with roundingMode set to .halfUp — it defaults to .halfEven). Add unit tests asserting the exact-tie cases (12.5%, 100.5, 0.125) against the Android strings, and a cross-surface fixture test shared with the watchOS target.

risks.risk: iOS cannot guarantee background execution, so the dashboard, complications and alert floor can go arbitrarily long without new data where Android's foreground service kept a 15-second cadence. Users migrating from Android will perceive this as the app 'stopping'.
risks.mitigation: Design for honesty rather than continuity: the ported freshness policy already greys out and badges stale values, and complications must carry pre-scheduled degrade entries so they never show a confident hours-old number. Layer notify-characteristic BLE delivery with Core Bluetooth state preservation and restoration, plus APNs push for backend-configured users. Set the expectation explicitly in onboarding copy and in the docs, because the failure mode is a product expectation problem, not a bug.

risks.risk: Core Bluetooth does not exist in the iOS Simulator, so every connection state in the status row, the entire pull-to-refresh read sequence, the pump-metric freshness tiers, and all pump-sourced chart and card data are unreachable in the developer's primary loop.
risks.mitigation: Build the simulated pump driver as a first-class Debug target dependency before building the dashboard, with recorded fixture histories covering the full 3H/24H/7D/30D range, all eight trend values, out-of-range and clock-skewed readings, and scripted connection-state transitions. Treat it as the reference implementation of the driver protocol, not as throwaway test scaffolding.

risks.risk: The iOS Simulator does not enforce Local Network Privacy, Data Protection classes, or WidgetKit/BGTaskScheduler budgets. Cleartext LAN backend access, before-first-unlock storage behaviour, and complication refresh starvation will all appear to work in the Simulator and fail only on hardware, often only after hours of real use.
risks.mitigation: Maintain a short on-device smoke checklist that must pass before every TestFlight upload: local-network permission prompt and denial path, app launch and complication render before first unlock, and a multi-hour complication soak. Budget exhaustion in particular is invisible until hardware.

risks.risk: WatchConnectivity between paired iPhone and Apple Watch simulators is functional but unreliable — session activation races, reachability and isWatchAppInstalled misreporting, and flaky file/complication transfers. The developer will validate the phone→Watch data and settings relay against a transport that behaves differently on hardware.
risks.mitigation: Use updateApplicationContext (coalescing, latest-wins, survives unreachability) for settings and current values rather than sendMessage, so the Simulator's reachability flakiness is not on the critical path. Validate the relay on paired hardware before relying on any Watch-facing acceptance criterion, and make the Watch app render an honest 'no data from phone' state rather than blanking.

risks.risk: Shipping Tandem, Medtronic and Nightscout brand marks in an App Store Connect binary. Apple's review of third-party trademarks is stricter and less predictable than Google Play's, and external TestFlight distribution goes through Beta App Review. A reviewer can read the marks as implying manufacturer affiliation or endorsement.
risks.mitigation: Keep the marks strictly nominative (no manufacturer name in the app name, icon, subtitle, keywords or screenshots), include a prominent unaffiliated-with-any-manufacturer disclaimer in the app and on the first launch screen, and keep the mark rendering behind a single asset lookup so all marks can be disabled with one change if review demands it. Prepare a written nominative-use justification for the review notes.

risks.risk: Apple has historically scrutinised diabetes apps under Guideline 1.4.1 (medical apps must not risk physical harm, and must be accurate). This app is read-only monitoring, which is materially lower risk than dosing apps, but the alert-floor 'this device is watching you' claim is exactly the kind of statement a reviewer will probe — especially given iOS cannot guarantee the background execution that would make it true.
risks.mitigation: Lead with the honesty design in the review notes: the app never claims to be watching unless it has a strictly-fresh reading, every stale value is visually de-emphasised, and no therapeutic write is possible. Ship the existing medical disclaimer prominently. Do not describe the app as an alarm or safety system in App Store Connect metadata.

risks.risk: There is no SF Symbol for Bluetooth, and the Bluetooth word mark and figure mark are Bluetooth SIG trademarks whose use is tied to SIG membership and a product Declaration ID. Substituting a generic radio-waves symbol degrades a status indicator whose meaning users learn from the published docs.
risks.mitigation: Ship a custom SF Symbol set with the four Bluetooth states so the glyph is under the project's control, and confirm the SIG membership and Declaration ID position for the product (the project already ships BLE, so the obligation exists independently of the icon). If the marks cannot be used, pick one substitute glyph family and update docs/mobile/status-icons.mdx for iOS rather than mixing metaphors.

risks.risk: Unicode paired-arrow glyphs U+21C8 and U+21CA may not be covered by SF Pro at 40pt bold, silently falling back to a different font and producing a visibly mismatched double-arrow next to the single arrows — on the single most-read element in the app.
risks.mitigation: Verify coverage at the shipped size and weight on device early. If the fallback is visible, ship a custom SF Symbol pair for the double arrows while keeping the Unicode string as the data contract, so the phone/Watch string equality with the Android trendSymbol implementation is preserved.

risks.risk: GlucoseColors are identical in light and dark, as on Android. Green #22C55E and Yellow #EAB308 on a white surface fall well short of WCAG AA contrast for small text, which affects the TIR legend entries, the CGM-stats assessment subtitles and the age caption in Light theme.
risks.mitigation: Keep the hues fixed (they are a cross-surface semantic contract with the web app and the Watch), but darken only the TEXT variants in the Light appearance via a paired 'onLight' colour set, leaving fills and dots at the canonical hue. Verify with the Accessibility Inspector's contrast check and with Increase Contrast enabled.

risks.risk: TestFlight builds expire after 90 days and external testing requires Beta App Review for each new version's first build, which conflicts with the fast iteration this dashboard will need. Internal-only testing (100 users, no review) has no such friction but a hard cap.
risks.mitigation: Automate build-and-upload in CI so the 90-day expiry is a non-event, keep an internal group for the developer's own loop, and batch external releases so Beta App Review is hit on a predictable cadence rather than per-commit.

risks.risk: The 5-second WhileSubscribed teardown grace window is load-bearing for rotation and navigation on Android, and it also controls when analytics 'since' timestamps re-anchor. Swift has no built-in equivalent, so a naive port using plain observation lifetimes will either re-query on every navigation (a visible flicker and a moving window) or never tear down (leaked observations and stale windows).
risks.mitigation: Implement a small ref-counted observation holder with an explicit 5-second teardown delay and test both behaviours: a sub-5-second round trip must not re-anchor the window, and a longer absence must.

questions_for_pm: When the iPhone is unreachable or suspended, what must the Apple Watch app still be able to show? On Android the watch is purely a relay fed by a phone foreground service, so the question never arose; on iOS the phone cannot guarantee it is running, so a straight relay port means the watch can go dark for hours in a way the Android watch does not. The three honest options are (a) accept a degraded watch that shows an explicit 'no recent data from phone' state, (b) let the watch fetch independently from the backend over its own Wi-Fi/LTE for backend-configured users only, or (c) let the watch connect to the pump directly over Core Bluetooth. Each is permitted by Apple and each changes scope materially, and the Android repo cannot answer it.
